# In Defense of Darkness

Try to remember the last time you experienced true darkness. Not the dimness of a bedroom with curtains drawn, not the amber hush of a city street at 3 a.m., but genuine darkness — the kind that erases your own hand when you hold it up before your face. For most of us, such moments are vanishingly rare. We live inside a permanent twilight of our own making, a glow that leaks upward from every streetlamp, billboard, and window until even the night itself has been domesticated.

Astronomers have a name for the result: light pollution. By their estimates, more than eighty percent of North Americans can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Globally, roughly a third of humanity — and nearly everyone in Europe and the United States — has lost sight of the galaxy we inhabit. Think about that: the great river of stars that every human who ever lived gazed upon, until about a century ago, is now a rumor, something you must travel to remote deserts and mountaintops to verify.

This is a strange thing to have lost, and stranger still that we barely noticed losing it. For nearly all of human history, night was a genuine frontier. When the sun went down, firelight made only a small island in the dark, and beyond its edge stretched a world belonging to the moon and stars. Those lights weren't decoration; they were infrastructure. Farmers read the seasons in them. Sailors steered by them. The stars told Polynesian navigators when to set out across open ocean; the heliacal rising of Sirius told Egyptian priests that the Nile would soon flood. And because there was little else to do in those long hours, the sky became our first cinema and our first scripture — every culture projecting its heroes, beasts, and gods onto those flickering points, telling stories across the fire about why the world was as it was.

Electric light gave us enormous gifts. It extended the working day, made streets safer, opened the night to reading, medicine, conversation. But like many gifts, it arrived quietly bundled with a cost nobody itemized. We didn't just illuminate the night; we displaced it. And displacement has consequences that reach far beyond nostalgia.

Consider first the body. Human physiology was tuned over hundreds of thousands of years to a planet that turned reliably between light and dark. Darkness triggers the release of melatonin, the hormone that governs sleep; the blue-white glare of screens and LEDs suppresses it. Chronic exposure to light at night scrambles our circadian rhythms, and through them, our health. We are, quite literally, built for a daily passage into darkness, and we keep canceling the trip.

Then consider the creatures whose lives depend on the dark. On beaches from Florida to Oman, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the moonlit sea. Now they crawl toward beachfront hotels and perish in parking lots. Migrating birds, navigating by stars they can no longer see, circle illuminated skyscrapers in confusion, dying by the hundreds of millions each year in collisions. Insects — moths especially, those devoted servants of the moon — spiral exhausted around our porch lamps. Whole ecosystems dim when the night does.

And yet the loss isn't merely biological. Something in us needed the dark, too. When Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from the window of his asylum in Saint-Rémy, he was working from memory and longing as much as observation — but the cypress tree and the swirling sky belong to a world where night still had a face. The Romantics walked out into it deliberately, seeking in darkness what daylight couldn't provide: awe, smallness, communion with something larger than themselves. Night was where imagination went to stretch.

There is a particular kind of thinking that happens only in the dark. With vision — our dominant sense — dialed down, attention turns inward. The dark removes surfaces and leaves essence. It is no accident that we associate it with both fear and intimacy: with monsters under the bed and with whispered conversations late into the night. The fear is ancient and honest; our ancestors had real reasons to dread what they couldn't see. But the other inheritance is just as old — darkness as shelter, as rest, as the great leveler where everything exposed in daylight grows equal and quiet.

A few places are trying to hand it back. There are now certified International Dark Sky Reserves — in Utah's canyon country, in New Zealand's Mackenzie Basin, on remote Atlantic islands — where local ordinances forbid excess lighting and visitors can once again lie on their backs beneath an unbroken bowl of stars. First-timers often expect the postcard version: blazing constellations on black velvet. What they actually get is subtler and stranger. Under a truly dark sky, the Milky Way doesn't shine so much as haunt — a pale, luminous rift overhead, so faint and so vast that newcomers sometimes mistake it for a cloud. Then the adjustment comes, and with it a quiet vertigo: the cloud is made of some two hundred billion suns, and we are looking at it from the inside.

Here is the deeper argument underneath all of this: a species that abolishes darkness may eventually forget what darkness is for. Light means knowledge, clarity, productivity, exposure — all fine things. But darkness is the necessary complement: rest, mystery, patience, the willingness not to know. A culture lit twenty-four hours a day begins to believe that everything worth seeing is already visible, that every question deserves an instant answer, that there is no proper time for anything except now. The dark sky argues otherwise. It rewards those who wait — twenty minutes, half an hour — while their eyes slowly reopen capacities they didn't know they had closed.

So consider this an invitation. Some clear, moonless night, walk to wherever the streetlights end. Switch off your flashlight and stand still. Let your eyes adjust; it takes longer than you think. Then look up and meet the one darkness we have left — the original one, older than fire, patient enough to wait for us to come back.
